pumac-2010-power-01a.title: Small cycles
pumac-2010-power-01a.body:
$C_1$ has the single edge $\{v_1,v_1\}$, a loop. $C_2$ has the edges $\{v_1,v_2\}$ twice (from $i=1$ and from $\{v_1,v_n\}$): parallel edges. For $n\ge3$ the $n$ edges $\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}$, $\{v_1,v_n\}$ are distinct pairs of distinct vertices, so $C_n$ is simple.

**Answer: exactly $n\ge3$**

pumac-2010-power-01b.title: Count
pumac-2010-power-01b.body:
$C_6$ has $6$ edges and the hub is joined to the $6$ rim vertices: $6+6=12$.

**Answer: 12**

pumac-2010-power-01c.title: Both directions
pumac-2010-power-01c.body:
We show $G$ is disconnected iff some pair $u\ne v$ has no path.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $u,v$ are distinct vertices with no path between them. Let $A$ be the set of vertices reachable from $u$ by a path (including $u$) and $B=V\setminus A\ni v$. Both are nonempty. If an edge joined $a\in A$ to $b\in B$, then a path from $u$ to $a$ followed by $b$ would be a path from $u$ to $b$ (all vertices on the path lie in $A$, so $b$ is new), giving $b\in A$, a contradiction. So there is no edge between $A$ and $B$ and $G$ is disconnected.

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $G$ is disconnected with parts $A,B$ and no edges between them; take $u\in A$, $v\in B$. A path from $u$ to $v$ starts in $A$ and ends in $B$, so some consecutive vertices $v_i\in A$, $v_{i+1}\in B$ are adjacent, contradicting the absence of edges between $A$ and $B$. So no path from $u$ to $v$ exists. ∎

pumac-2010-power-01d.title: Remaining vertices
pumac-2010-power-01d.body:
The remaining $n-1$ vertices are still pairwise adjacent and no loops or parallel edges appear, so the result is $K_{n-1}$.

**Answer: $K_{n-1}$**

pumac-2010-power-01e.title: Classify by whether the hub is deleted
pumac-2010-power-01e.body:
$W_{2010}$ has the hub $h$ and a rim cycle on $2010$ vertices.

**Hub deleted** (and two rim vertices): what remains is the rim cycle minus two vertices, a disjoint union of two paths with $a$ and $b$ vertices, $a+b=2008$, $0\le a\le b$ (the case $a=0$ is a single path). The unordered pair $\{a,b\}$ determines the graph and vice versa: $a=0,1,\dots,1004$, i.e. $1005$ graphs.

**Hub kept** (three rim vertices deleted): the remaining $2007$ rim vertices form arcs (paths) of sizes $a,b,c\ge0$ with $a+b+c=2007$, and the hub is adjacent to all of them. Rotations and reflections of the rim can realise every permutation of $(a,b,c)$, so the graph depends only on the multiset $\{a,b,c\}$; conversely the multiset is recovered from the graph (remove the unique vertex adjacent to all others; the remaining paths have sizes $a,b,c$). Hence the number of graphs equals the number of partitions of $2007$ into at most $3$ parts, which is the nearest integer to $\frac{(2007+3)^2}{12}=\frac{2010^2}{12}=336675$, i.e. $336675$.

A graph with the hub deleted is a path forest with $2008$ vertices and at most $2007$ edges, while a graph with the hub kept has at least $2007$ edges from the hub plus rim edges, so the two families are disjoint.

Total: $336675+1005=337680$.

**Answer: 337680**

pumac-2010-power-01e.title: Check by computer on small wheels
pumac-2010-power-01e.body: The same count for $W_n$ is $p_{\le3}(n-3)+\lfloor\frac{n-2}2\rfloor+1$; for $n=8,9,10,11,12,13,14$ it gives $9,11,13,15,18,20,23$, which agrees with a direct isomorphism-by-isomorphism enumeration of all $\binom{n+1}3$ ways to delete three vertices.

pumac-2010-power-01f.title: Only the empty graph
pumac-2010-power-01f.body: $K_1$ is a single vertex. Any graph with at least one vertex has $K_1$ as a subgraph (delete all other vertices). So $G$ has $n=0$ vertices, hence no edges: $0\le-n=0$. ∎

pumac-2010-power-02a.title: Edge counts and the definition
pumac-2010-power-02a.body:
(a) $W_4$ has $8$ edges, $W_3$ has $6$. Contracting an edge removes that edge and keeps every other edge (as an edge, a parallel edge or a loop), so $G/e$ always has exactly one edge fewer than $G$: it would have $7\ne6$. **False.**

(b) For a loop $e=\{v,v\}$ ($u=v$ in the definition), $G/e$ replaces $v$ by a new vertex $\varepsilon$ carrying exactly the edges that $v$ had, except $e$; this is $G$ with $e$ removed. **True.**

pumac-2010-power-02b.title: Proof
pumac-2010-power-02b.body:
Note the third condition says: for $u\ne v$, at least as many edges of $G$ join $f(u),f(v)$ as edges of $H$ join $u,v$; for $u=v$, $E(f(u),f(u))-|f(u)|\ge(\#\text{loops at }u)-1$, i.e. the number of edges inside $f(u)$ exceeds a spanning tree's $|f(u)|-1$ by at least the number of loops at $u$.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Induction on the number $k$ of operations. For $k=0$, $H=G$ and $f(v)=\{v\}$ works. Suppose $H$ is a minor of $G_1$ via a map $f_1$ and $G_1$ comes from $G$ by one operation.
* $G_1=G\setminus x$ (vertex deleted) or $G\setminus e$ (edge deleted): $f=f_1$ works in $G$; connectivity of $G|_{f(v)}$ and the edge counts can only increase.
* $G_1=G/e$ with $e=\{u,v\}$ and new vertex $\varepsilon$: define $f(x)=f_1(x)$ if $\varepsilon\notin f_1(x)$, and $f(x)=(f_1(x)\setminus\{\varepsilon\})\cup\{u,v\}$ otherwise. Then $G|_{f(x)}$ is connected ($u,v$ are adjacent via $e$ and every edge at $\varepsilon$ comes from an edge at $u$ or $v$), the sets stay disjoint, and each edge of $G/e$ comes from a distinct edge of $G$ while the edge $e$ is an extra edge inside $f(x)$ and $|f(x)|=|f_1(x)|+1$; so all three conditions persist.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Given $f$, delete all vertices outside $\bigcup f(v)$. For each $v$, contract the $|f(v)|-1$ edges of a spanning tree of the connected graph $G|_{f(v)}$; the set $f(v)$ becomes one vertex and the other edges inside it become loops, of which there are $E(f(v),f(v))-(|f(v)|-1)\ge\#\text{loops at }v$ in $H$. Edges between $f(u)$ and $f(v)$ ($u\ne v$) become parallel edges between the two new vertices, at least as many as in $H$. Delete the surplus loops and parallel edges: the result is $H$. ∎

pumac-2010-power-02c.title: Go through the nine cases
pumac-2010-power-02c.body:
(a) **Yes**: delete three vertices of $K_8$.
(b) **No**: $K_{2,2}$ has only $4<5$ vertices (minors never gain vertices).
(c) **No**: $K_{3,3}$ has $9<10$ edges (an edge count of $K_5$ cannot be reached; deleting/contracting never adds edges).
(d) **Yes**: contract three disjoint edges $a_ib_i$ ($i=1,2,3$) of $K_{4,4}$; the three merged vertices are pairwise adjacent (via $a_ib_j$), and $a_4$, $b_4$ are adjacent to each other and to all three merged vertices: $K_5$.
(e) **Yes**: $K_{5,5}\supseteq K_{4,4}$.
(f) **No**: every minor of $C_{125}$ has all degrees $\le2$ (contractions in a cycle only produce shorter cycles or loops); $K_5$ has degree $4$.
(g) **Yes**: $W_3=K_4$.
(h) **Yes**: contract two rim edges of $W_5$, which gives $W_3=K_4$.
(i) **No**: $W_6$ is planar (draw the hub in the middle of the hexagon), minors of planar graphs are planar (5.2), and $K_5$ is not planar (5.1).

pumac-2010-power-02d.title: Counting branch sets
pumac-2010-power-02d.body:
(a) Use the branch sets of 2.2. In a $K_{2010}$ minor all $2010$ branch sets are pairwise adjacent. A branch set that is a single vertex lies in one of the two sides of $K_{n,n}$, and two singleton branch sets in the same side are not adjacent; so at most $2$ branch sets are singletons and the other $2008$ have at least $2$ vertices: $2n\ge2+2\cdot2008=4018$, $n\ge2009$. Conversely, in $K_{2009,2009}$ contract the $2008$ disjoint edges $a_ib_i$ ($i\le2008$): the merged vertices are pairwise adjacent, and $a_{2009},b_{2009}$ are adjacent to each other and to every merged vertex. So $n=2009$.

(b) $W_{2010}$ has $2011$ vertices, and $K_{n,n}$ has $2n$, so $2n\ge2011$, $n\ge1006$. In $K_{1006,1006}$ contract one edge $a_1b_1$: the merged vertex is adjacent to all other $2010$ vertices, and the remaining vertices $\{a_2,\dots,a_{1006},b_2,\dots,b_{1006}\}$ induce $K_{1005,1005}$, which has a Hamiltonian cycle. So $W_{2010}$ is a subgraph of the contracted graph. Hence $n=1006$.

**Answer: 2009 and 1006**

pumac-2010-power-02e.title: One-line argument
pumac-2010-power-02e.body: If $G$ had an edge $\{a,b\}$ ($a\ne b$ since $G$ is simple), deleting all vertices other than $a,b$ gives $K_2$ as a minor. So $G$ has no edges. ∎

pumac-2010-power-03a.title: Complete graph on 4 vertices
pumac-2010-power-03a.body: In $K_4$ any two vertices are adjacent, so in a partition into colour classes with no two adjacent vertices in the same class every class has at most one vertex; three classes hold at most $3<4$ vertices. So $K_4$ is not $3$-colourable. ∎

pumac-2010-power-03b.title: Forests
pumac-2010-power-03b.body: Let $G$ be simple with no $K_3$ minor. If $G$ contained a cycle $v_1,\dots,v_k$ (distinct vertices, $k\ge3$, since $G$ is simple), contracting $k-3$ edges of the cycle and deleting the other vertices and edges would give $K_3$ as a minor. So $G$ has no cycle: it is a forest. Colour each tree (by components) by the parity of the distance from a chosen root; adjacent vertices have different parity. So $G$ is $2$-colourable. ∎

pumac-2010-power-03c.title: Disjoint loops
pumac-2010-power-03c.body: Let $G$ consist of $n$ vertices, each carrying a single loop: $n>n-1$ edges. There are no edges between distinct vertices, and deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges (a loop contraction just removes the loop) never creates an edge between two distinct vertices. But $K_3$ has edges between distinct vertices; so $K_3$ is not a minor. ∎

pumac-2010-power-04a.title: Check each graph
pumac-2010-power-04a.body:
* $K_4$: draw a triangle with the fourth vertex in the middle joined to the three corners. Planar.
* $C_4$: a square. Planar.
* $W_4$: a square with its hub in the middle joined to the four corners. Planar.
* $K_{4,4}$ contains $K_{3,3}$, which is not planar (5.1). Not planar.
* The picture: the drawing has an apparent crossing, but the graph has the three edges $T\!-\!L$, $T\!-\!B$, $L\!-\!R$, i.e. it is the path $R-L-T-B$; redraw it as a path without crossings. Planar (a graph is determined by its vertices and edges, not by one drawing).

pumac-2010-power-04b.title: Minimal counterexample
pumac-2010-power-04b.body:
Suppose the claim fails and take a counterexample $G$ with $n$ as small as possible and, for that $n$, the fewest edges: $G$ is simple, has no $K_4$ minor and $e\ge2n-2$ edges. For $n=3$ there are at most $3=2n-3$ edges, so $n\ge4$.

*Degree $\le2$.* If $v$ has degree $\le2$, then $G-v$ has $n-1\ge3$ vertices, no $K_4$ minor, and by minimality at most $2(n-1)-3$ edges; so $e\le2n-5+2=2n-3$, a contradiction.

*A vertex of degree $3$.* Let $v$ have neighbours $x,y,z$. They are not pairwise adjacent (else $K_4\subseteq G$), say $x\not\sim y$. Contract the edge $vx$ and merge parallel edges: the only possible common neighbour of $v$ and $x$ is $z$, so at most $1+1=2$ edges are lost. The new simple graph has $n-1\ge3$ vertices, no $K_4$ minor and at least $e-2\ge2n-4>2(n-1)-3$ edges, contradicting minimality.

*All degrees $\ge4$.* Then $e\ge2n$; deleting any edge gives a smaller counterexample (same $n$, $e-1\ge2n-1\ge2n-2$ edges), contradiction.

So no counterexample exists. ∎

pumac-2010-power-05a.title: Euler's formula
pumac-2010-power-05a.body:
In a plane drawing of a simple connected graph with at least $3$ vertices, every face is bounded by at least $3$ edge-sides and each edge contributes exactly $2$ edge-sides (counting an edge twice when the same face is on both sides). So $2E\ge3F$.

$K_5$: $V=5$, $E=10$; Euler gives $F=7$, and $2E=20<21=3F$. Contradiction.

$K_{3,3}$: $V=6$, $E=9$, $F=5$. $K_{3,3}$ has no odd cycles (it is bipartite) so every face has at least $4$ edge-sides: $2E=18\ge4F=20$ is false. Contradiction. ∎

pumac-2010-power-05b.title: Minors of planar graphs are planar
pumac-2010-power-05b.body: Let $G$ be planar, drawn without crossings. Deleting a vertex or an edge keeps the drawing crossing-free. To contract an edge $e=\{u,v\}$, slide $u$ along $e$ towards $v$, dragging all edges at $u$ with it; the edges remain non-crossing and in the end $u$ and $v$ coincide, giving a crossing-free drawing of $G/e$ (the other edges between $u,v$ become loops). So every minor of a planar graph is planar. If $G$ had a $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$ minor, that planar minor would contradict 5.1. ∎

pumac-2010-power-05c.title: Characterisation
pumac-2010-power-05c.body:
Loops and parallel edges are irrelevant for path minors, so work with the simplification. A path $P$ of length $3$ is connected, so it is a minor of $G$ iff it is a minor of one connected component.

Let $G$ be connected and simple with $m$ vertices.
* If $m\le3$: $P$ has $4$ vertices and a minor never has more vertices than the graph, so no $P$ minor.
* If $m\ge4$: take a spanning tree $T$. If $T$ contains a path of length $3$, that path is a subgraph, hence a minor. Otherwise $T$ has no path with $3$ edges, so its diameter is $\le2$ and $T$ is a star with centre $c$ and $m-1\ge3$ leaves. If $G$ has an extra edge $\{x,y\}$ between two leaves, take a third leaf $z$: $z,c,x,y$ is a path of length $3$. So $G$ has no $P$ minor iff $G=T$ is a star.

A star (with extra loops and parallel edges) has no $P$ minor: every minor of a star is a disjoint union of stars (deleting keeps stars; contracting a centre–leaf edge gives a star; contracting a loop or parallel edge is a deletion), and $P$ is not a union of stars (no vertex of $P$ is adjacent to all three others). ∎

pumac-2010-power-05d.title: Edges of the two graphs
pumac-2010-power-05d.body:
A $K_2$ subgraph is an edge together with its ordered identification of ends. All edges of $K_{2,3}$ are equivalent, each joining a vertex of the $2$-side to one of the $3$-side (two possible orientations of the identification). $W_4$ has two kinds of edges: *spokes* (hub–rim, with the ends distinguishable) and *treads* (rim–rim, the two ends interchangeable by a symmetry of $W_4$). Gluing along a tread gives one graph; gluing along a spoke gives two graphs, according to whether the hub is identified with the vertex from the $2$-side or the $3$-side of $K_{2,3}$. So there are at most $3$ graphs, and one checks (e.g. by comparing degree sequences or by a computer isomorphism test) that these three are pairwise non-isomorphic: all have $8$ vertices and $12$ edges.

**Answer: 3**

pumac-2010-power-05e.title: Proof
pumac-2010-power-05e.body:
Let $S$ be a $k$-sum, $k\le2$, glued along $C$ ($|C|=k$), let $G'=V(G)\setminus C$, $H'=V(H)\setminus C$; there are no edges between $G'$ and $H'$ in $S$. If $G'$ or $H'$ is empty then $S$ is a subgraph of $H$ or $G$ and we are done, so assume both nonempty. Suppose $S$ has a $K_{3,3}$ minor with branch sets $B_1,\dots,B_6$ (disjoint, connected, with $B_i,B_j$ adjacent whenever $i,j$ lie on opposite sides of $K_{3,3}$).

At most two branch sets meet $C$. Delete them from $K_{3,3}$: the remaining $\ge4$ vertices of $K_{3,3}$ still induce a connected graph ($K_{3,3}$ minus any two vertices is connected). The corresponding branch sets are connected and avoid $C$, so each lies in $G'$ or in $H'$, and adjacent ones lie on the same side; hence they all lie in $G'$, say (the case $H'$ is symmetric).

Now define $B_i^*=B_i\cap(G'\cup C)$ for every $i$. *Connectedness in $G$:* a branch set $B_i$ meeting $C$ may contain vertices of $H'$; but $B_i\cap(G'\cup C)$ consists of pieces of $G'$ each attached to a vertex of $C\cap B_i$, and if $C\subseteq B_i$ the two vertices of $C$ are adjacent in $G$ ($C$ is a clique of $G$). So $B_i^*$ is connected in $G$. *Adjacency in $G$:* if $B_i,B_j$ are adjacent through an edge of $S$ with an endpoint in $H'$, then both $B_i,B_j$ contain a vertex of $C$ (the endpoint in $H'$ forces its set to meet $C$, and the other end lies in $H'\cup C$ so its set meets $C$ too), say $c_i\in B_i$, $c_j\in B_j$; these are adjacent in $G$ as $C$ is a clique. Otherwise the edge is an edge of $G$ already. Hence the $B_i^*$ are branch sets of a $K_{3,3}$ minor of $G$, contradiction. ∎

pumac-2010-power-05f.title: Counterexample
pumac-2010-power-05f.body:
$K_5$ and $K_4$ have no $K_{3,3}$ minor (they have only $5$ and $4<6$ vertices). Glue a triangle $\{a,b,c\}$ of $K_5$ to a triangle of $K_4$ and delete its edges. The result has the six vertices $a,b,c,p,q,r$, where $p,q$ (from $K_5$) and $r$ (from $K_4$) are each adjacent to all of $a,b,c$, and $p\sim q$. It contains $K_{3,3}$ with parts $\{a,b,c\}$ and $\{p,q,r\}$ as a subgraph, hence as a minor. So the statement fails for $3$-sums.

**Answer: No**

pumac-2010-power-05g.title: Minimal counterexample
pumac-2010-power-05g.body:
Take a counterexample with $n$ minimal and then $e$ minimal: no $K_5$ minor, $e\ge3n-5$. For $n=4$, $e\le6=3n-6$, so $n\ge5$.

*Degree $\le3$:* deleting such $v$ leaves $n-1\ge4$ vertices and (by minimality) $\le3(n-1)-6=3n-9$ edges, so $e\le3n-6$: contradiction.

*Degree $4$:* the neighbours of $v$ are not pairwise adjacent (else $K_5$), so some neighbour $u$ is nonadjacent to another neighbour $w$ and has at most $2$ neighbours among the remaining neighbours. Contract $uv$: the common neighbours of $u,v$ are at most $2$, so at most $3$ edges are lost. The new simple graph has $n-1\ge4$ vertices, no $K_5$ minor and $\ge e-3\ge3n-8=3(n-1)-5$ edges: a smaller counterexample.

*All degrees $\ge6$:* $e\ge3n$; deleting an edge gives a smaller counterexample.

*So some vertex $v$ has degree exactly $5$* (all degrees are $\ge5$, not all $\ge6$). Let $u_1,\dots,u_5$ be its neighbours. If some $u_i$ is adjacent to at most $2$ of the other four, contracting $u_iv$ loses at most $1+2=3$ edges, a smaller counterexample as before. So every $u_i$ is non-adjacent to at most one other $u_j$; the non-adjacent pairs form a matching, contained in $\{u_1u_2,\ u_3u_4\}$ after relabelling. Contract the edge $u_1u_3$ to a vertex $w$: $w$ is adjacent to $u_2$ (via $u_3$), $u_4$ (via $u_1$), $u_5$, and $v$; and $u_2,u_4,u_5$ are pairwise adjacent and adjacent to $v$. So $\{v,w,u_2,u_4,u_5\}$ gives a $K_5$ minor, contradiction. ∎

pumac-2010-power-06a.title: Set-up
pumac-2010-power-06a.body:
Suppose the claim fails. Choose a counterexample $G$ (simple, no $K_6$ minor, $e>4n-10$) with $n$ minimal and then $e$ minimal. If $e\ge4n-8$ we could delete an edge and still have a counterexample, so $e=4n-9$. Since $K_5$ has only $10=4\cdot5-10$ edges, $n\ge6$. Graphs with fewer than $n$ vertices and no $K_6$ minor satisfy the bound (for $\ge5$ vertices).

**Step 1: every edge $uv$ lies in at least $4$ triangles.** Contract $uv$ and merge parallel edges: the resulting simple graph $G'$ has $n-1\ge5$ vertices and no $K_6$ minor, so $e(G')\le4(n-1)-10$. Also $e(G')=e-1-c$ where $c=|N(u)\cap N(v)|$. Hence $c\ge e-1-(4n-14)=4$.

**Step 2: $\delta(G)\ge5$.** A vertex $v$ of degree $0$ could be deleted ($e=4n-9>4(n-1)-10$). If $v$ has a neighbour $u$, then $v$ has at least $4+1$ neighbours (the $\ge4$ common neighbours with $u$ plus $u$). Moreover: if $\deg v=5$, each neighbour $u$ has $4$ common neighbours with $v$, i.e. is adjacent to all four other neighbours, so $N(v)\cup\{v\}$ is a $K_6$: contradiction. So $\delta(G)\ge6$.

**Step 3: there is no clique $S$ with $|S|\le3$ such that $G-S$ is disconnected.** Suppose $V=A\cup S\cup B$ with $A,B\neq\varnothing$ and no $A$–$B$ edges, $S$ a clique, $|S|=s\le3$. Put $n_1=|A|+s$, $n_2=|B|+s$. A vertex of $A$ has degree $\le n_1-1$, so $n_1\ge7$ (as $\delta\ge6$), similarly $n_2\ge7$; both are $<n$. By minimality $e(G[A\cup S])\le4n_1-10$ and $e(G[B\cup S])\le4n_2-10$, and since $n_1+n_2=n+s$,
$$e\le4(n+s)-20-\tbinom s2\le 4n-11<4n-9$$
(for $s=3$; smaller $s$ gives even less), a contradiction.

**Step 4: the average degree.** $\sum\deg=2e=8n-18<8n$, so some vertex $v$ has degree $\le7$, hence $6$ or $7$. Let $N=N(v)$ and $W=V\setminus(N\cup\{v\})$. By Step 1 every vertex of $N$ has at least $4$ neighbours in $N$. For a component $Q$ of $G[W]$, its neighbourhood $N(Q)\subseteq N$, and $Q\cup\{p\}$ is connected for every $p\in N(Q)$. If $p,q\in N(Q)$ are non-adjacent, contracting the connected set $Q\cup\{p\}$ to the single vertex $p$ gives a minor of $G$ whose part on $N\cup\{v\}$ is $G[N\cup\{v\}]$ with the extra edge $pq$. ($\ast$)

**Step 5: $\deg v=6$ is impossible.** Every vertex of $N$ ($6$ vertices) is adjacent to $\ge4$ of the other $5$, so the non-adjacent pairs inside $N$ form a matching $M$. If $|M|\le2$ we get a $K_6$ minor directly: for $|M|=0$ it is a $K_6$ subgraph; for $|M|=1$ delete an end of the missing pair and keep $v$; for $|M|=2$ with missing pairs $a_1a_2$, $b_1b_2$ contract the edge $a_1b_1$ — the merged vertex is adjacent to $a_2,b_2$ and to everything else, and together with $a_2,b_2$ and the remaining two vertices of $N$ and $v$ we get $6$ pairwise adjacent vertices. So $|M|=3$, with non-adjacent pairs $a_1a_2$, $b_1b_2$, $c_1c_2$. If $W=\varnothing$ then $n=7$ and $e\le21-3=18<19$, contradiction. Otherwise take a component $Q$ of $G[W]$. If $N(Q)$ contained both vertices of some pair, by ($\ast$) the pair becomes adjacent and $|M|$ drops to $2$: a $K_6$ minor, contradiction. So $N(Q)$ contains at most one vertex of each pair: it is a clique of size $\le3$ and $G-N(Q)$ is disconnected ($Q$ is separated from $v$), contradicting Step 3.

**Step 6: $\deg v=7$ is impossible.** Every vertex of $N$ is adjacent to $\ge4$ of the other $6$, so the graph $F$ of non-adjacent pairs inside $N$ has maximum degree $\le2$: a disjoint union of paths and cycles on $7$ vertices. Such an $F$ is contained in one of $C_7$, $C_6\cup K_1$, $C_4\cup C_3$, $C_3\cup C_3\cup K_1$, or contains a $5$-cycle (i.e. is $C_5$ or $C_5\cup K_2$). Label the vertices $0,\dots,6$ of $N$; in each case the complement of $F$ has a $K_5$ minor, with branch sets (the five sets are connected and pairwise adjacent in the complement):
* $F\subseteq C_7$ (cycle $0123456$): $\{0,3\},\{1,5\},\{2\},\{4\},\{6\}$;
* $F\subseteq C_6\cup K_1$ (cycle $012345$): $\{0,2,4\},\{1\},\{3\},\{5\},\{6\}$;
* $F\subseteq C_4\cup C_3$ (cycles $0123$, $456$): $\{0,4\},\{1\},\{2,5\},\{3\},\{6\}$;
* $F\subseteq 2C_3\cup K_1$ (triangles $012$, $345$): $\{0,3\},\{1,4\},\{2\},\{5\},\{6\}$;
* $F=C_5$ (cycle $01234$): $\{0,1,3\},\{2\},\{4\},\{5\},\{6\}$.
(One checks each pair of sets contains an adjacent pair in the complement.) Together with $v$, adjacent to all of $N$, this is a $K_6$ minor. The only remaining case is $F=C_5\cup K_2$ (cycle $01234$ and the pair $\{5,6\}$). Then $G[N]$ is the pentagonal bipyramid: the vertices $0,\dots,4$ induce a $5$-cycle, and $5,6$ are non-adjacent and adjacent to all of $0,\dots,4$; its largest clique has size $3$. If $W=\varnothing$ then $n=8$ and $e\le7+15=22<23$, contradiction. Otherwise let $Q$ be a component of $G[W]$. If $N(Q)$ contained a non-adjacent pair $p,q$, by ($\ast$) removing that pair from $F$ leaves $F-pq\subseteq C_7$ (a linear forest) or $F-pq=C_5$, which has a $K_5$ minor, hence a $K_6$ minor with $v$: contradiction. So $N(Q)$ is a clique, of size $\le3$, and separates $Q$ from $v$, contradicting Step 3.

**Conclusion.** By Steps 2, 5, 6 every vertex has degree $\ge8$, so $e\ge4n>4n-9$, contradicting Step 4 (average degree $<8$). Hence no counterexample exists. ∎

pumac-2010-power-07a.title: Construction
pumac-2010-power-07a.body:
Let $G$ have a clique $K$ on $5$ vertices and an independent set $I$ of $n-5$ vertices, each adjacent to all of $K$ (and to nothing else). It is simple, has $10+5(n-5)=5n-15$ edges.

Suppose it had a $K_7$ minor with branch sets $B_1,\dots,B_7$ (disjoint, connected, pairwise adjacent). At most $5$ of them meet $K$, so at least $2$ lie entirely inside $I$. A connected subset of the independent set $I$ is a single vertex, and two such singleton branch sets are not adjacent: contradiction. ∎

pumac-2010-power-08a.title: Construction
pumac-2010-power-08a.body:
Let $G$ be $K_{10}$ with the edges of a perfect matching ($5$ disjoint edges) removed: $n=10$, $45-5=40>6\cdot10-21=39$ edges, simple.

Suppose $G$ had a $K_8$ minor with $8$ branch sets inside $10$ vertices. Then at least $6$ of the branch sets are single vertices (the surplus is only $2$ vertices), and these $6$ vertices must be pairwise adjacent in $G$. But a set of pairwise adjacent vertices of $G$ contains at most one end of each of the five removed edges, hence has at most $5$ vertices: contradiction. ∎
